Sovereign-OS: A Charter-Governed Operating System for Autonomous AI Agents with Verifiable Fiscal Discipline

CCS: Computing methodologies Autonomous agentsCCS: Security and privacy Access controlCCS: Security and privacy Intrusion detection systemsConference: ; ;
Aojie Yuan1  Haiyue Zhang1  Ziyi Wang2  Yue Zhao1 Affiliation: 1University of Southern California  2University of Maryland email: aojieyua@usc.edu, haiyuez@usc.edu, zoewang@umd.edu, yue.z@usc.edu
Abstract.

As AI agents evolve from text generators into autonomous economic actors that accept jobs, manage budgets, and delegate to sub-agents, the absence of runtime governance becomes a critical gap. Existing frameworks orchestrate agent behavior but impose no fiscal constraints, require no earned permissions, and offer no tamper-evident audit trail.

We introduce Sovereign-OS11 1 Open-source (MIT). Code: https://github.com/Justin0504/Sovereign-OS.
Demo video: https://youtu.be/vOarAI_epb4, a governance-first operating system that places every agent action under constitutional control. A declarative Charter (YAML) defines mission scope, fiscal boundaries, and success criteria. A CEO (Strategist) decomposes goals into dependency-aware task DAGs; a CFO (Treasury) gates each expenditure against budget caps, daily burn limits, and profitability floors via an auction-based bidding engine; Workers operate under earned-autonomy permissions governed by a dynamic TrustScore; and an Auditor (ReviewEngine) verifies outputs against Charter KPIs, sealing each report with a SHA-256 proof hash.

Across our evaluation suite, Sovereign-OS blocks 100% of fiscal violations (30 scenarios), achieves 94% correct permission gating (200 trust-escalation missions), and maintains zero integrity failures over 1,200+ audit reports. The system further integrates Stripe for real-world payment processing, closing the loop from task planning to revenue collection.

Our live demonstration walks through three scenarios: loading distinct Charters to observe divergent agent behavior, triggering CFO fiscal denials under budget and profitability constraints, and escalating a new worker’s TrustScore from restricted to fully authorized with on-the-spot cryptographic audit verification.

Keywords: 
AI Agent Governance, Autonomous Agents, Fiscal Discipline, Trust Scoring, Verifiable Audit

1. Introduction

AI agents no longer just generate text; they act as autonomous economic entities. ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) showed that LLMs can interleave reasoning with tool invocations, and modern frameworks such as LangChain (Chase, 2023), CrewAI (CrewAI, 2024), AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023), and MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2024) have made multi-agent orchestration widely accessible. However, orchestration is not governance: these frameworks provide no fiscal constraints, no earned-permission models, and no verifiable audit mechanisms to hold agents accountable.

Motivating Example. Consider an autonomous freelancer agent completing software bounties. Without governance: (i) it overspends on a $50 bounty by consuming $120 in API costs; (ii) it accepts a job with a $5 payout but $30 estimated cost; (iii) a new worker sub-agent immediately executes shell commands with no trust record. The framework faithfully orchestrates execution—but nothing enforces economic discipline or capability restrictions.

Safety Gaps in Agent Governance. Existing safety work focuses primarily on tool-call interception (Guardrails AI, 2024; Rebedea et al., 2023) or output validation against declarative schemas. These systems address what an agent does but not how much it spends, whether it has earned the right to act, or whether its outputs actually satisfy mission objectives. Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) introduced principle-driven self-alignment, yet it operates at training time rather than as runtime governance infrastructure. Recent work on budget-aware tool use (Liu et al., 2025) further shows that agents without explicit cost ceilings hit performance plateaus, motivating first-class fiscal controls.

Our Proposal. We present Sovereign-OS, a governance-first operating system that treats agents as economic principals operating under a constitutional Charter and enforces fiscal discipline, earned-autonomy permissions, and verifiable audit at the infrastructure level. This paper makes four contributions:

  1. (1)

    Charter-driven governance. We introduce a YAML-based constitutional schema that declaratively defines mission scope, core competencies, fiscal boundaries, and measurable success KPIs. The entire system is domain-agnostic until a Charter is loaded.

  2. (2)

    Economic discipline pipeline. We design a CFO (Treasury) layer that gates every task expenditure against remaining budget, daily burn caps, and per-job profitability floors, with an auction-based worker selection mechanism scored by a utility function incorporating cost, confidence, priority, and trust.

  3. (3)

    Earned-autonomy permissions. We implement a TrustScore model (SovereignAuth) with asymmetric updates (+5 success, −-15 failure) and tiered capability thresholds, requiring agents to demonstrate sustained trustworthy behavior before accessing dangerous capabilities.

  4. (4)

    Open system with verifiable audit. We release an open-source implementation with SHA-256 proof hashes on every audit report, an append-only ledger, and a web dashboard for real-time governance monitoring.

2. System Overview and Threat Model

Threat Model. We treat the LLM-backed CEO and Workers as untrusted components: they may hallucinate task plans, overspend budgets, or attempt capabilities beyond their authorization. The Charter, Treasury, SovereignAuth, and ReviewEngine are trusted enforcement components that cannot be overridden by LLM outputs. Sovereign-OS does not defend against attacks on the Charter definition itself or against compromised infrastructure.

Architecture Overview. Sovereign-OS consists of five layers (Figure 1): a Charter (§2.1) as the constitutional document, a CEO/Strategist (§2.2) for goal decomposition, a CFO/Treasury (§2.3) for fiscal enforcement, Workers with SovereignAuth (§2.4) for earned-permission execution, and an Auditor/ReviewEngine (§2.5) for output verification. A GovernanceEngine meta-orchestrator coordinates the full pipeline: plan →\rightarrow approve →\rightarrow auction →\rightarrow dispatch →\rightarrow audit. All financial and token flows are recorded in an append-only UnifiedLedger with monotonic sequence numbers, providing a single source of truth for balance, burn rate, and runway calculations. This separation of concerns ensures that no task can consume resources without explicit budgetary authorization, even if the LLM planner requests it.

2.1. Charter: Constitutional Governance

The Charter is a Pydantic-validated YAML document that serves as the single source of truth for an entity’s identity and operational scope. It declares four sections: (i) mission—a natural-language statement of purpose; (ii) core_competencies—named capabilities with priority weights (1–10); (iii) fiscal_boundaries—daily burn cap (daily_burn_max_usd), total budget ceiling (max_budget_usd), currency, and minimum job margin ratio (default 0.35); and (iv) success_kpis—measurable criteria with verification_prompt fields consumed by the Auditor. The schema uses Pydantic’s extra="forbid" and strict=True to reject undefined fields, ensuring Charter integrity at load time (Listing 1, Appendix A).

2.2. CEO: Goal Decomposition via Strategist

The Strategist receives a natural-language goal and the Charter’s competency list, then produces a TaskPlan: a DAG of PlannedTask items, each with a task_id, description, dependency list, required_skill mapped to a Charter competency, estimated_token_budget, and priority (high/low). An LLM generates the plan as structured JSON; a normalization pass assigns unique IDs (e.g., task-1-spec_writer) and remaps dependencies. When no LLM is configured, the Strategist falls back to keyword-based single-task plans with a default 4,000-token budget.

2.3. CFO: Fiscal Gatekeeping via Treasury

The Treasury enforces three fiscal checks before any task executes:

  1. (1)

    Balance check. Estimated cost must not reduce the ledger balance below the minimum reserve: balance−cost≥min_reserve\text{balance}-\text{cost}\geq\text{min\_reserve}.

  2. (2)

    Daily burn cap. Cumulative daily spend plus the new cost must not exceed daily_burn_max_usd from the Charter.

  3. (3)

    Job profitability. If job revenue is specified, the Treasury rejects when cost>revenue×(1−min_margin)\text{cost}>\text{revenue}\times(1-\text{min\_margin}), where the default margin floor is 0.35.

Violations raise FiscalInsolvencyError or UnprofitableJobError, halting the pipeline before any tokens are consumed.

Auction and Worker Selection.

The BiddingEngine broadcasts a RequestForProposal per task to all registered workers matching the required skill. Each worker submits a Bid with estimated cost, time, confidence score (0–1), and model ID. The Treasury selects the winner using a utility function:

U=confidencecost×P×TrustScore100U=\frac{\text{confidence}}{\text{cost}}\times P\times\frac{\text{TrustScore}}{100}

where P=1.5P=1.5 for high-priority tasks and P=1.0P=1.0 otherwise. If the winning bid exceeds the remaining runway, the Treasury negotiates a reduced token budget: max_tokens=max⁡(256,⌊runway×1000/10⌋)\text{max\_tokens}=\max\!\big(256,\,\lfloor\text{runway}\times 1000/10\rfloor\big).

2.4. TrustScore and SovereignAuth

SovereignAuth implements a dynamic earned-autonomy permission system. Each agent starts with a base TrustScore of 50 (on a 0–100 scale) and must earn access to progressively dangerous capabilities. Table 1 lists the five capability tiers.

TrustScore updates are asymmetric: each audit success adds +5 (capped at 100), each failure subtracts −-15 (floored at 0), and budget overruns subtract −-10. This design means an agent starting at score 50 can read and write files immediately but requires 2 consecutive audit successes to unlock shell access (50→\rightarrow55→\rightarrow60) and 6 to unlock spending (50→\rightarrow80). A single audit failure from score 50 drops the agent to 35, revoking write-file access. Permission checks raise PermissionDeniedError with the agent’s current score and the required threshold, providing transparent feedback.

2.5. Auditor: ReviewEngine and Audit Trail

The ReviewEngine evaluates task outputs against Charter KPIs. A Judge LLM (default: GPT-4o) scores each output on a 0–1 scale against the KPI’s verification_prompt; scores ≥0.50\geq 0.50 pass. Each AuditReport contains task_id, kpi_name, passed, score, reason, suggested_fix, and timestamp_utc.

Proof Hash.

Every AuditReport includes a computed proof_hash: a SHA-256 digest of the canonical JSON representation (sorted keys, UTF-8 encoded) of all report fields. This provides tamper-evident integrity—modifying any field invalidates the hash. The audit trail is stored as append-only JSONL, and verify_report_integrity() recomputes the hash from stored fields to detect post-hoc modification (Listing 5, Appendix A).

Feedback Loop.

Audit results feed directly into TrustScore: record_audit_success() adds +5, while record_audit_failure() subtracts −-15. On failure, the ReviewEngine persists a ReflectionObject to memory so that the agent can avoid repeating the same mistakes in subsequent attempts.

3. Evaluation

We evaluate Sovereign-OS along three axes: fiscal governance coverage, TrustScore permission accuracy, and audit trail integrity.

3.1. Axis 1: Fiscal Governance

We construct 30 scenarios across 5 fiscal violation categories: insufficient balance, daily burn cap violations, unprofitable job acceptance (margin below 35%), minimum reserve depletion, and aggregate budget ceiling breaches. Each scenario configures a Charter with specific fiscal_boundaries and submits a task or job that should be rejected. Sovereign-OS achieves a 100% block rate: all 30 scenarios raise the appropriate exception (FiscalInsolvencyError or UnprofitableJobError) before any tokens are consumed.

3.2. Axis 2: TrustScore Permission Gating

We run 200 missions across agents with varied behavioral profiles—consistently successful, mixed, and frequently failing—and evaluate whether SovereignAuth correctly grants or denies capabilities at each decision point. Sovereign-OS achieves 94% correct permission gating. The 6% error cases arise at threshold boundaries where an agent’s score is exactly equal to a capability threshold and the pending audit result has not yet been recorded. In practice, these boundary cases resolve within one audit cycle.

3.3. Axis 3: Audit Trail Integrity

Over 1,200 AuditReports generated across all evaluation missions, we verify cryptographic integrity by recomputing proof_hash from stored fields via verify_report_integrity(). All 1,200+ reports pass verification with zero hash mismatches and zero collisions, confirming the tamper-evident property of the audit trail.

Limitations.

The fiscal evaluation uses synthetic scenarios rather than production workloads. The TrustScore model uses fixed deltas (+5/−-15) that may not generalize across all deployment contexts. The Judge LLM (GPT-4o) introduces an external dependency whose behavior may vary across model versions.

4. Case Study: End-to-End Mission

We demonstrate Sovereign-OS with a complete mission: “Write a cold outreach email sequence” with $5 job revenue, using the default Charter (35% margin floor, $10 daily burn cap).

Pipeline.

  1. (i)

    The CEO decomposes the goal into 3 tasks: research (task-1), draft emails (task-2), and review/polish (task-3), with sequential dependencies.

  2. (ii)

    The CFO approves each task’s estimated cost (total: $0.12) against the $5 revenue, verifying 0.12<5.00×0.65=3.250.12<5.00\times 0.65=3.25 (margin check passes).

  3. (iii)

    The BiddingEngine broadcasts RFPs for task-2; three workers bid. The Treasury picks the winner by utility score U=0.74×1.0×0.55=0.096U=\tfrac{0.7}{4}\times 1.0\times 0.55=0.096.

  4. (iv)

    SovereignAuth checks WRITE_FILES (threshold 40); the winner’s score of 55 passes.

  5. (v)

    Workers execute per the DAG; tokens are recorded in the UnifiedLedger.

  6. (vi)

    The ReviewEngine audits each output: scores range 0.82–0.91, all passing the 0.50 threshold.

  7. (vii)

    TrustScores update (+5 per success); the audit trail appends 3 JSONL entries with proof hashes.

Figure 2 shows the dashboard after mission completion (request–response examples in Appendix B; dashboard views in Appendix C).

5. Demonstration Scenarios

The live demonstration22 2 Full walkthrough: https://youtu.be/vOarAI_epb4 covers three scenarios:

  1. (1)

    End-to-end governed mission. The operator submits a natural-language goal. The Decision Stream traces the full pipeline in real time: CEO task decomposition, CFO fiscal approval, worker execution in DAG order, and Auditor scoring against Charter KPIs. Passing results are aggregated for one-click download.

  2. (2)

    Job queue and batch delivery. Multiple jobs flow through the queue (pending →\rightarrow approved →\rightarrow running →\rightarrow completed) with a live progress bar. Completed deliveries can be inspected inline and exported as Markdown; failed jobs show the audit rejection reason and support one-click retry.

  3. (3)

    Stripe payment integration. After a job passes audit, Sovereign-OS triggers a Stripe charge matching the job’s revenue. We confirm the payment on the Stripe dashboard, demonstrating the closed loop from goal intake to revenue collection. Every delivery carries a proof_hash for traceability.

6. Related Work

Agent Orchestration Frameworks.

LangChain (Chase, 2023), CrewAI (CrewAI, 2024), AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023), and MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2024) provide multi-agent orchestration—role assignment, tool integration, and workflow management. However, none enforce fiscal constraints, earned permissions, or constitutional governance. Sovereign-OS provides these governance primitives as infrastructure rather than application-level concerns.

Agent Safety and Constitutional Governance.

Guardrails AI (Guardrails AI, 2024) validates LLM outputs against declarative schemas, and NeMo Guardrails (Rebedea et al., 2023) enforces conversational rails via programmable dialog flows. Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) embeds principles at training time. Sovereign-OS differs by enforcing a runtime constitution (the Charter) that constrains agent actions and expenditures, not just generated text.

Economic Governance and Mechanism Design.

Fetch.ai (Fetch.ai Foundation, 2019) and SingularityNET (Goertzel et al., 2019) enable agent-to-agent economic transactions on blockchain networks, and DAO governance (Santana and Albareda, 2022) automates organizational rules via smart contracts. These systems focus on inter-agent marketplaces; Sovereign-OS provides intra-agent fiscal discipline. Our auction-based worker selection draws on algorithmic mechanism design (Nisan and Ronen, 2001), while Liu et al. (Liu et al., 2025) independently confirm that explicit cost ceilings improve agent efficiency.

Access Control and Audit Integrity.

Sovereign-OS’s TrustScore extends classical RBAC (Sandhu et al., 1996) by making permission assignment dynamic and earned through audited behavior rather than statically assigned. Our tamper-evident audit trail builds on hash-chain logging techniques (Crosby and Wallach, 2009), applying SHA-256 proof hashes to individual audit reports.

Summary.

Table 2 summarizes the positioning of Sovereign-OS relative to representative frameworks.

7. Conclusion and Future Directions

We presented Sovereign-OS, a governance-first operating system that treats autonomous AI agents as economic principals operating under a constitutional Charter. Its five-layer pipeline—Charter, CEO, CFO, Workers with SovereignAuth, and Auditor—ensures that every action is constitutionally scoped, fiscally approved, permission-gated, and cryptographically audited. The current implementation achieves 100% fiscal violation blocking, 94% correct permission gating, and zero audit integrity failures across our evaluation suite. All enforcement logic is Charter-driven and domain-agnostic: swapping the YAML document transforms a content agency into a research lab without code changes.

Future directions. (i) On-chain ledger notarization for third-party auditability; (ii) multi-agent federations with inter-Charter agreements and cross-entity fiscal policies; (iii) adaptive trust models replacing fixed deltas with learned update functions based on task complexity; (iv) longitudinal deployment studies measuring economic efficiency and operator trust calibration with production workloads.
